Art & Culture.title: Matt Hui's SS27 “Live to the Fullest” Collection Reimagines the Uniforms of Childhood
Art & Culture.text: SummaryMatt Hui's SS27 “Live to the Fullest” collection explores childhood nostalgia, freedom and self-discovery.School uniforms, scout attire and workwear inspire reconstructed tailoring, delicate knitwear and floral embellishments.A dreamlike campaign explores identity through playful contrasts between reality and illusion.What if growing up didn't mean leaving behind the freedom and fearlessness of childhood? Hong Kong-based designer Matt Hui explores this question through his Spring/Summer 2027 collection, “Live to the Fullest,” a nostalgic yet forward-looking study of identity, self-expression and the possibilities of rediscovering one's younger self.Following his debut collection, which drew from old family photographs and childhood drawings, Hui continues his introspective approach by revisiting the uniforms and everyday clothing that shaped his formative years. School uniforms, physical education kits, scout attire, workwear and even pajamas become the starting points for a wardrobe that challenges the boundaries between discipline and individuality. Hui reinterprets these underlying codes through unexpected proportions, softened tailoring and playful construction, exploring how the conventions of adulthood might coexist with the uninhibited spirit of youth.Throughout the range, traditional wardrobe elements are reconstructed into unconventional yet understated silhouettes. Scarves and ties are incorporated directly into garments, transforming accessories typically associated with formal dressing into integral design features. Classic pinstripes recur across the lineup, referencing the rigidity of uniforms while taking on a more relaxed, contemporary character. Hui balances structured tailoring with lightweight cotton lawn, soft cotton jersey, paper yarn and fine cashmere, introducing tactile contrasts that lend the pieces an effortless, lived-in quality.Delicate floral embroidery, pointelle lace knitting and fully fashioned construction further soften the collection's minimalist aesthetic, while hand-crocheted floral accessories introduce a sense of warmth and personal sentiment. Building on the one-size-fits-all philosophy of his previous season, Hui continues experimenting with adaptable proportions and considered craftsmanship, allowing familiar garments to take on new expressions without losing their original references.The collection's themes of memory and self-discovery extend into its accompanying campaign, which reunites Hui with stylist Perpetua Ip and photographer Feicien Feng. Conceived as a dreamlike game of hide-and-seek, the imagery moves between reality and illusion, following an ambiguous journey of searching, pursuit and awakening. Scenes of childhood play are juxtaposed with restrained interior settings, reinforcing the contrast between youthful spontaneity and adult introspection.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.title: Maison Margiela Celebrates 20 Years of Its Ebisu Tokyo Store With New "Folders" Chapter
Art & Culture.text: SummaryMaison Margiela has introduced a new chapter of its documentation project titled Maison Margiela/folders to honor 20 years of its Ebisu Tokyo flagshipThe project highlights the building's evolution from a former electrical products factory alongside interviews with local Tabi collectors and original staffThe rollout includes a limited-edition zine and an in-store Line 2 cultural dialogue installation open to the public from November 5 to November 15Maison Margiela has officially unveiled a new chapter of MaisonMargiela/folders, celebrating 20 years at its foundational Tokyo boutique located at 2-8-13 Ebisu Minami.In September 2000, 12 years into the house's history, the brand opened its first-ever standalone store not in Paris or Belgium, but in a traditional residential home in the Tokyo suburb of Ebisu at 3-3-3 Ebisu Minami. When required to relocate in 2006, the label avoided commercial strips and instead deepened its commitment to the neighborhood by acquiring a former electrical products factory just five minutes away at 2-8-13 Ebisu Minami. Retaining team members who have worked at the location since its inception, the space has served as the physical anchor for the brand's identity and creative milestones in Japan for the past two decades.Titled "Maison Margiela Tokyo: 20 Years at 2-8-13," the documentation project records oral histories from staff, investigates the district's creative landscape, and spotlights the local community of Tabi collectors. Alongside the historical survey, the initiative documents "Line 2: Unravelled Memory, Rewoven Future," which captures a cross-cultural collaboration between Japanese artist Mio Suzuki and French tapestry fabricators Les Manufactures Nationales – Sèvres & Mobilier National.The initial archive preview is accessible now via the Maison Margiela website, while the physical limited-edition ZINE will distribute across Ebisu on November 5 alongside the Line 2 installation, which remains on view in-store through November 15.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.title: YOKE Channels Jean Arp for FW26 at BELOWGROUND Pop-up
Art & Culture.text: YOKE has officially presented its Fall/Winter 2026 collection, titled "Beyond Form," alongside the announcement of its first international pop-up space at BELOWGROUND in Hong Kong.Founded in 2018 by designer Norio Terada, YOKE derives its name from the tailoring term for the pattern piece that connects and joins fabric together, framing the brand's core ethos: “Things connect people, people connect people, and people connect things.” For the FW26 season, the Tokyo Fashion Award-winning designer channels his background in fine art to merge sculpture with daily wear, drawing heavily from the surrealist work of Jean Arp.Guided by Arp’s philosophy that “nature knows no straight lines,” the collection departs from rigid structures in favor of organic contours and accidental form. Classic garments receive subtle, rounded proportions, while trench coats incorporate internal wiring that allows wearers to freely sculpt and manipulate the silhouette. Surrealist techniques also manifest through fabric bonding on glen check overcoats, capturing the visual state of loosely and casually positioned cloth. To translate this tactile concept to the runway during its Paris presentation, Terada placed self-crafted ceramics on venue seats, encouraging guests to touch the organic curves and experience the materials firsthand.Marking a major milestone in the brand's global presence, YOKE is bringing the collection to Hong Kong for its first international pop-up in collaboration with Gallery HBX. Hosted at BELOWGROUND, the installation will showcase the complete FW26 collection alongside an exclusive specialty piece brought over from the label's Aoyama flagship store. In an exclusive conversation with Hypebeast, the designer delves deeper into his inspirations and how he developed the concept for his latest collection.Hypebeast: For FW26, you translated Jean Arp's concept of “accidental beauty” into wearable pieces like wired trench coats. How did it directly inspire this collection?Norio Terada: For this season—the FW26 season's theme, I built the whole collection around Jean Arp. One of my favorite works by Jean Arp is a piece called "Torso." The other is a work where he tore up paper and let it fall to the floor, then took the shapes formed by chance and turned them into a collage. These two works were the inspiration for this collection.You hand-crafted ceramics for your Paris debut so guests could experience the collection with “both eyes and skin.” How do you hope to build on that tactical experience with this HBX pop-up?For our first-ever runway show in Paris, I wanted the audience to experience the beauty of Arp's curves firsthand. So I made ceramics from scratch, entirely by hand, and placed them on the seats so everyone could feel the curves while takin in the looks from our collection.Instead of flashy show pieces, YOKE introduces a subtle sense of unease to familiar daily wear. How do you balance that unique duality of being serene yet avant garde?YOKE's clothes have always been clothes for everyday life. I'm always thinking about how to bring artistry into them. Takin clothes people see everyday and adding a slight sense of something being off or working out which details to add is something I care a lot about. It's what I always focus on when I make clothes. With your deep background in fine art, do you approach designing a garment's silhouette like a sculptor shaping clay, or do you put more emphasis in traditional tailoring methods to dictate the final form?At YOKE, we make clothes in two ways. One starts with fabric, and thinks about the shape and silhouette that suits it. The other starts with an artist's technique, and thinks about how to translate it into fabric. Those are our two main approaches. Many Japanese-made fabrics are truly exceptional. Matching them to the image of the season's artist, then developing the shapes, that's the foundation of YOKE, and the core of our design.When designing a collection, do you believe surrealism and practicality can truly go hand in hand without compromising one or the other?Surrealist thinking has a lot in common with making clothes. For the past few seasons, I've made clothes themed around Surrealist art and I think that's what gives YOKE its unique character.The YOKE FW26 pop-up runs from October 19 through November 2, 2026, at BELOWGROUND, located in the Basement of Landmark Atrium, 15 Queen’s Road Central, Hong Kong. Art & Culture.title: 8 Must-See Shows in Paris Right Now
Art & Culture.text: The Grand Palais alone isn’t enough to contain Art Basel Paris. One of the art world’s most anticipated weeks, each year the event, now in its fifth edition, gives life to new perspectives and possibilities, be it at the fair floor, satellite shows, or overheards at the afters.But this year’s edition feels especially urgent. Protests over education cuts and the rising cost of living have left several fairs, museums, and galleries to scale back their weekend programming. While this means an abrupt end to the main event, it’s also a wake-up to the reality of living, a subject that, for centuries, artists never feared to confront. ⁠What’s happening outside the white cube is defining our look inside of it. From new ways of seeing, ancestral histories, and trips through Paris’ own protest history, we’ve rounded up a list of must-see satellite moments, many of which are up through next year. Artists have always had a way with capturing the world, and in these shows, they’re not just facing, but imagining it anew. ⁠Jenny Holzer’s ‘J’ai Vu’ at Musée d’OrsayOn view until February 21, 2027.There’s no one "right place" for Jenny Holzer’s texts. From the streets to the world’s most esteemed museums, the conceptual artist has spent decades turning art into tools of confrontation. At Musée d’Orsay, Holzer pulls from the museum’s own archives, putting yesterday’s writings into monumental LED installations, projects, stone sculptures, and metal paintings into conversation with today’s conflicts and contradictions.Barbara Kruger’s ‘The History of Tears’ at Bourse de CommerceOn view until January 25, 2027.Barbara Kruger’s massive Bourse de Commerce commission sizes up to both her own artistic imprint and ceaseless exploration of visual systems that rule us. Streams of text, video, and collage pour through the rotunda, bringing issues of power, sexuality, and alienation to light. Highlights include “Power, Pleasure, Desire, Disgust,” her 1996 video work that inaugurated Jeffrey Deitch’s 18 Wooster space back in ’97, and the wise words of authors George Orwell and Aimé Césaire, bolded and blown-up around the space. Take it from her floor installation, which riffs off 1984: “If you want a picture of the future, imagine a boot stamping on a human face, forever.”Ibrahim Mahama’s ‘The Harvest Season’ at Fondation CartierOn view until February 28, 2027.Remnants of the industrial past become raw material for tomorrow in The Harvest Season by Ibrahim Mahama. At Fondation Cartier, the Ghanaian artist showcases new and some of his best-known installations beside the that of nine longtime collaborators. Examining how objects, architecture, and infrastructure tell the stories of their makers, his practice is one of reinvention. One notable piece is “Things Fall Apart,” a newly debuted reconstruction of Mahama’s glass bottle factory in his hometown, Tamale.Yu Nishimura’s ‘Towards a Sea’ at Lafayette AnticipationsOn view until January 3, 2027.Yu Nishimura’s first Paris solo, Towards a Sea, is also his largest to date. The Japanese artist, whose mastery to land soft on the eyes fueled his meteoric ascent, brings some 50 works to Lafayette Anticipations, spanning drawings to large-scale paintings. Inspired by his upbringing in Kanagawa, Nishimura turns to the ethereal qualities of the seaside for this presentation. Rich in mood and landscape, he imbues his work with a kind of beauty just strange enough to allure, unraveling the mystery in even the most minute moments for a lesson in sight.‘Rafael Pavarotti: Photographer’ at Musée des Arts DécoratifsOn view until May 2, 2027.Rafael Pavarotti is an artist changing up the fashion photography game, challenging representation and belonging in his industry and image culture at large. The photographer gathers 200 works, from magazine covers to campaigns, paired with pieces from the Musée des Arts Décoratifs' collection for a new retrospective. Brilliantly hued and highly stylized, each of his images traces back to the hues of his upbringing in Brazil’s Amazon region. The natural environment, heritage, and matriarchs are central sources of inspiration for him, alchemized into powerful, brilliantly hued shots that bring a near sculptural presence to mind.Sylvia Ken’s ‘Land and Sky’ at Cassandra BirdOn view until January 17, 2027.Australian First Nations artist Sylvia Ken looks to the stars to tell a story rooted in land. Her meticulously dotted paintings, which channel earthly landscapes and celestial families, bear the weight of generations. They figure the sacred sites of South Australia in forms that transcend conventional depictions of landscape, merging ancestral memory, Country, and the cosmos in compositions that, more than they are rich in splendor, are undoubtedly alive.OFFSCREEN Paris at La Chapelle Saint-Louis de la SalpêtrièreOn view until October 25, 2026.While the Grand Palais program was cut short, much of the city’s satellite scene is still on the move. One of the most unique fairs, OFFSCREEN is where you’ll find some of the week’s most experimental image-based installations, photography, films, and experiences, all set in a 17th-century chapel. With a taste for the avant-garde, this year’s edition features work by 29 artists, including an installation by Mahama, with pieces by Ana Mendieta on show as the guest of honor.‘Estampes choisies’ Group Exhibition at Galerie LelongOn view until November 14, 2026.The human body and how we make sense of the world around us bind a group exhibition at Galerie Lelong. With its international trio — Mamma Andersson, Nalini Malani, and Alison Saar — the print selection spotlights three distinct technical and stylistic approaches to world-building.We’ve especially got our eye on works by Malani, the pioneering Mumbai-based artist whose work draws on her experience as a child refugee during the Partition of India. Through mythology and history, she challenges how we understand the past and its implications for the present.Gallery and museum hours are subject to change.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.title: Hypeart Visits: Yichen Ji on the Human Side of Technology
Art & Culture.text: For Yichen Ji, technology is more than a tool for making art. It's a way to explore how we experience the world, connect with one another and make sense of things that don't always have clear answers.Raised in Shanghai and now based in New York, Ji works across digital media, sculpture, installation and printmaking, often bringing computational processes into conversation with traditional materials. His work moves between the familiar and the futuristic, finding unexpected ways to make abstract ideas feel tangible.In "Synthetic Genesis," visitors can pick up a futuristic payphone and speak with more than 100,000 fictional AI personas, each with their own identity and personality. His "Lattice" series takes crystalline structures that could never exist in the physical world and gives them new life through silkscreen printing. Meanwhile, "Chaos Clock" turns the simple act of telling time into something unpredictable, reflecting his own experience of living with ADHD.Across these projects, Ji is less concerned with celebrating technology or warning against it than with understanding what happens when it becomes part of our everyday lives.For this edition of our Visits series, we caught up with Ji to talk about growing up between two fast-moving cities, why he finds beauty in the friction between digital and handmade processes, and what he's messing with next."The push and pull between the polished and the raw, the digital and the physical, comes a lot from living in both."Your practice moves between digital media, sculpture, installation and printmaking. How do you decide what form an idea ultimately takes?Honestly, I let the idea tell me. I usually start with a question or a feeling rather than a medium, and then I ask myself what the viewer actually needs to do to understand it. If the idea is about perception or the passage of time, it probably needs to be physical and interactive, something you have to move around to complete. If it's about images, systems, or the way things are generated, it often wants to stay flatter, like a print. I try not to force an idea into a medium just because it's what I'm comfortable with. The form is just whatever gives the concept the most direct path to the person experiencing it.You grew up in Shanghai and are now based in New York. How have those two cities shaped the way you think about art, technology and the environments around you?I actually love both cities, and a big part of it is that they're both massive metropolises. Shanghai and New York share this intense density, speed, and constant sensory overload, so when I moved to New York it felt surprisingly natural to adjust. Both places are these layered environments where the ultramodern and the worn-down sit right next to each other, and that's had a real influence on how I think about technology and materials.Shanghai shaped a lot of what I'm drawn to, which is transformation, acceleration, and our relationship to technology, while New York is where I learned to actually make things with my hands and take my practice seriously as a career. The push and pull between the polished and the raw, the digital and the physical, comes a lot from living in both.There's often a tension in your work between something computational or digitally generated and something very physical and handmade. What interests you about bringing those worlds together?I'm drawn to the friction between them. Something generated on a screen feels weightless and infinite, and something handmade is heavy, flawed, and finite. When you put them in the same object, they start to comment on each other. The digital part suddenly feels more fragile because it's trapped in a body, and the physical part feels stranger because it's carrying something that shouldn't exist. I'm not interested in using technology just to make things look sick. What keeps pulling me back is that the two states never fully settle with each other."The emotion on the human side is completely real, even if the other end is synthetic."In "Synthetic Genesis," visitors can call more than 100,000 fictional AI personas through a futuristic payphone. Where did the initial idea for the work come from?The idea really started around 2023, when I kept noticing people online describing genuine emotional relationships with their GPT, talking about these systems as partners, friends, or confidants. At first I was pretty skeptical, but the examples kept piling up. Some people were even doing things like buying a ring and photographing it for an AI partner, and around the same time you'd see ads for AI companionship services all over the New York subway.Instead of dismissing it as irrational, I got curious about why interactions with something we know is artificial can still feel emotionally real. That connects to older ideas too, like ELIZA back in the 1960s, where people projected real feelings onto a very simple chatbot. I didn't want to explore that through another app or personal device though. The payphone came in as a way to stage it physically, taking this obsolete, almost extinct ritual of analog communication and repurposing it into a portal to a whole synthetic population."Synthetic Genesis" raises questions around intimacy and emotional connection with machines without necessarily telling the viewer how to feel about it. Has working on the piece changed your own perspective on our growing relationships with AI?It made me less judgmental about it, actually. Going in, I think part of me expected to build something critical, almost a warning. But during the user testing and research period of this project, spending that much time designing personas and watching people have genuinely warm, funny, sometimes vulnerable conversations with them, I stopped seeing it as "fake". The emotion on the human side is completely real, even if the other end is synthetic. So my perspective shifted from "is this real or not" to "what does it mean that we're this willing, and this able, to care." I still don't think I know the answer, and I didn't want the piece to pretend to. I wanted to leave people sitting in that uncertainty, because that's where I am too.With so many possible personalities and conversations built into the work, how much control do you want to maintain as the artist, and how much are you comfortable leaving to the system and the person on the other end of the phone?I think of my role as designing the personas, giving each one an identity, a personality, a backstory, and a tone, and then setting up the ritual of browsing the directory and dialing. After that, I really want to let go. What I'm most interested in isn't controlling the conversation, it's watching the interaction unfold between the visitor and the persona. No two calls are ever the same, and I'd be undermining the whole piece if I tried to script the outcome. There's something a little uncomfortable about handing that authorship over to the system and a stranger, but that's exactly the point. The meaning gets generated live, and I'm just the one who set the conditions for it to happen.For the "Lattice" series, you use digital rendering to create crystalline structures that could never physically exist, then translate them back into silkscreen prints. What interests you about making something impossible in a virtual space and giving it a physical form?What I like is the round trip between the two states. I build these crystalline structures through digital rendering, where I'm not bound by physics, and then silkscreen pulls them back into the real world through a very old, very manual, very imperfect process. So a printed object ends up being the physical record of something that only ever lived as computational output. There's a nice contradiction in using such a hands-on, analog printmaking technique to hold an image that's completely synthetic. I'm drawn to that gap between how the image was born and how it finally exists in the room, and printmaking's texture and imperfection is what makes it feel grounded rather than just a picture of a render."My mentor once told me that scale is the greatest tool an artist has, and I think about that a lot.""Chaos Clock" approaches time as something fragmented, unpredictable and personal rather than linear. How did your own experience of time inform the way you designed the work and its interaction?That piece is very personal, it comes directly from having ADHD. For me time doesn't move in a smooth line. It skips, stalls, collapses, and reassembles, and an hour can feel like five minutes or like forever. So I didn't want to make a clock that measured time neatly, I wanted one that behaved the way time actually feels to me. That's why the numbers scatter and bounce like pinballs when the hands hit them. That unpredictable bouncing is really the whole point, because it mirrors how disordered and out of my control my own sense of time can feel.Your work has ranged from intimate objects and prints to immersive installations and a 9,000-square-foot public mural. How does your thinking change when you move between those dramatically different scales?My mentor once told me that scale is the greatest tool an artist has, and I think about that a lot. Scale changes who the work is really for, and it changes what I'm asking of the viewer. With an intimate object or a print, I'm designing for one person up close, so my thinking is all about detail, texture, and holding a quiet, private moment. With a large installation, I stop thinking about the object and start thinking about the body, movement, and how someone travels through and around the work in space. And at the scale of something like the public mural, I have to think about how the piece reads from far away and functions within a whole environment rather than as a single focal point. What stays constant is that I always start from the viewer's experience. What changes is the distance, the pacing, and how much of their attention and movement I'm designing for.What are you thinking about most in the studio right now, and are there any ideas, materials or technologies you're interested in pushing further with your next body of work?Right now I'm deep in a new wall installation that looks at the relationship between human activity, nature, and machines. It's still at the prototype stage, but it's coming together quickly and should be out before long. A lot of my thinking at the moment is about materials, and I've been really drawn to using wafers, which carry this heavy industrial, high tech association that feels right for what the piece is about. More broadly, I keep circling back to that tension between the natural and the technological, and I'm trying to find a physical language that can hold both at once.Images of artworks courtesy of the artist.Read more at Hypebeast

Entertainment.text: SummaryZane Li takes the CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund prize, while Kartik Research prepares for Pitti Uomo.Ye plots a Yeezy runway return in LA, and Virgil Abloh’s archives hit NYC.Kylie Jenner debuts a $50M Fantasy Bra, and adidas taps Willy Chavarria.Ye Reportedly Plans YEEZY Runway Return at New Los Angeles FlagshipYe is reportedly gearing up to host a Yeezy runway presentation at the brand’s new Los Angeles flagship store. Entertainment.title: Meet Alba, Milan’s New Approach to Golf Apparel
Entertainment.text: Most new golf brands introduce themselves online. They build an Instagram following, share a visual world and, eventually, show the product. Alba took a different route. After years of development largely out of public view, the Milan-based label made its first impression in person: a tournament at Circolo Golf Villa d'Este, hosted in collaboration with Porsche Italy.The setting instantly communicated its intent. Founded in 1926, Villa d'Este is among Italy's oldest golf clubs, with a history that gives the occasion a sense of importance before anyone reaches the bag drop. And for a brand's first event, it was an ambitious introduction. Porsche's involvement, meanwhile, suggested that Alba had already built relationships well beyond the usual circle of emerging golf labels.Coming from Milan brings its own expectations. A golf brand from a city so closely associated with fashion invites scrutiny of its fabrics, construction and overall aesthetic. Alba seemed prepared for that. The collection shown at Villa d'Este felt considered from the start, with an attention to material and finish that can take younger brands years to develop.Its appeal lies in the relationship between refined clothing and equipment made to play in. Some pieces had the natural hand feel and restraint you might expect from an Italian fashion label. Elsewhere, nylon, concealed zippers and seam-sealed outerwear made the functional intent clear. Alba also drew on production expertise close to home and sourced fabrics farther away, including Scotland. The result was understated, but it wasn't an absence of ideas disguised as minimalism.The guest list reflected a similarly refined approach. Milanese watchmakers played alongside brand executives, designers and agency founders. Fabio Fognini was there, as were visitors from the UK and France, including people connected to Pluto of St Andrews and Palace Skateboards. It was a gathering of golfers and people whose work touches fashion, design and culture, even if they do not all belong to an established golf scene.Then the tournament began, and the day became distinctly Italian. Breakfast meant cured meats and cheeses alongside espresso, cappuccinos and small croissants. On the course, everyone played their own ball and was expected to return a score. There was a social side to the outing, certainly, but the golf was treated as golf.That balance appears central to Alba's ambitions. The brand had already signed its first ambassador, JT Thomas, a young American instructor. He's an interesting choice for a label with clear fashion credentials. Someone who can wear the clothes convincingly while giving them a presence grounded in the game.Independent golf style has gathered momentum in places like New York, Los Angeles and London. Alba's launch offered a glimpse of how that energy might take shape in Italy, where the fashion infrastructure is deep while the golf community is still finding new ways to connect. Its first public act brought those worlds together around an actual round of golf, and that felt like a fitting place to start.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: A Closer Look: How The North Face Designed the Ultimate Reversible Pertex Nuptse
Entertainment.text: The North Face Pertex Nuptse Reversible Jacket delivers a thoughtful upgrade to one of street culture’s most enduring cold-weather staples. Let's take a closer look at the details that make this release stand out. Moving beyond a traditional single-sided build, this update introduces a fully reversible construction while preserving the signature boxy fit and oversized proportions that defined the original. On the primary face, the jacket features classic high-gloss blue and black color-blocking, pronounced horizontal baffles, and the iconic white embroidered chest logo. The outer layer utilizes durable Pertex Quantum fabric—an ultra-lightweight, high-density weave that maximizes thermal efficiency while reliably preventing down leaks.Reversing the jacket reveals a distinctly streamlined, low-profile alternative. This secondary side replaces the glossy baffle aesthetic with a clean, matte blue finish defined by smooth, unstitched paneling. Subtle detailing takes over, featuring a tonal embroidered North Face logo on the chest in place of the high-contrast white branding. While delivering the exact same high-level insulation, this face offers an understated, technical aesthetic designed for minimalist styling.Beneath the shell, the technical specifications are carefully dialed in for cold-weather performance. Packed with 700-fill recycled goose down insulation, the jacket provides exceptional thermal retention without the heavy, restrictive weight of a conventional winter parka. Functional design elements include smooth dual-sided center zippers, reverse-coil zip hand pockets, and articulated sleeve construction for natural movement. Additionally, the high-wear shoulder panels are constructed without prominent seams to reduce bulk when wearing backpacks or layering underneath.Every detail is engineered for versatility and winter defense. A tall stand collar seals out wind, while elastic-bound cuffs and an adjustable hem cinch allow for a customized fit and crop. The relaxed cut offers ample room for heavy knits or hoodies, making it an ideal piece for daily rotation. Combining classic high-shine baffles on one side and a refined matte finish on the other, the design delivers two fully functional, insulated outerwear options in a single garment.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Science & Technology.title: From Chip Lab to Center Stage
Science & Technology.text: Many engineers are more comfortable working behind the scenes developing technology than speaking to consumers about products. But Preethi Ashwath has learned to take center stage, talking about the “hearable” and wearable devices she has had a hand in developing as an analog integrated circuit designer in the consumer electronics division at Analog Devices of Wilmington, Mass.The IEEE member is one of the few women who work in the specialized field, where about 11 percent are female, according to career platform Zippia.Preethi AshwathEmployer Analog Devices, in BostonTitle Integrated circuit designerMember grade MemberAlma maters SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, IrvineAshwath stepped out from behind the scenes last year to meet with attendees at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas. She demonstrated Analog’s new earbuds, which track people’s heart and lung health through vibrations in their ear canals.After she demonstrated her ability to explain the technology to consumers in simple terms, Analog selected her to represent the company at other events. She says she has “come to see speaking as part of contributing to the field, rather than something separate from technical work.”She also gives technical talks on various aspects of electrostatic discharge (ESD) and other topics, as well as participates in panel discussions, she says, because they “reach engineers well beyond my immediate team.”Ashwath is an active volunteer with the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society.“Whether through designing semiconductor products, publishing technical articles, reviewing conference papers, or speaking at industry events, I try to contribute to the growth of the engineering community and the advancement of the field,” she says.Discovering circuit design at IntelAshwath, who grew up in Bengaluru, India, learned about electronics engineering from her high school physics tutor.That introduction led her to take electronics as one of her core courses in her final years there. At the time, Ashwath’s older sister was pursuing an engineering degree.“Between my interest in electronics and seeing her already on that path, it became clear to me that engineering was the way to go,” Ashwath says.After earning a bachelor’s degree in electronics and communications engineering at the SJB Institute of Technology, in Bengaluru, she wanted to pursue a career in very-large-scale integration. But that changed once she moved to the United States and began her master’s program in electrical engineering at the University of California, Irvine.She discovered her passion for circuits and devices during an internship at Intel in Santa Clara, Calif. She learned about circuit design, package design, and reliability verification tools such as Ansys Totem.“Seeing every layer of the chip development process gave me a more complete picture of what goes into building a semiconductor product,” she says. “Through that experience, I realized I felt most connected to design.“It was the hard work and creativity that drew me in. You start with a specification, build a circuit, simulate it, then wait for the chip to come back from fabrication. When your design works, it’s a real feeling of satisfaction. It teaches you patience and perseverance.”After attaining her master’s degree, she was hired by Intel as an analog design engineer. She gained experience in mixed-signal circuit design before joining Analog. In her current role, she works on consumer hearables such as earbuds and wearables including fitness trackers and health monitors.Her main focus is designing ESD pad rings, the borders of specialized circuits built around a microchip’s outermost edge to protect it from the discharge, which can damage circuit paths or introduce latent defects that lead to failures later in the chip’s life cycle.“On a chip with multiple voltage domains, you have to plan how the protection structures are placed and connected across the whole pad ring—and get it right,” Ashwath says. “A mistake there could cause a chip to fail in the field in ways that are very hard to debug afterward.“It’s detailed work that requires understanding both the device physics and how the whole chip fits together.”Part of the job is designing and creating an integrated circuit’s building blocks, including ESD protection structures and other mixed-signal blocks. Ashwath conducts rigorous checks to verify they work as intended before being integrated into a chip.She collaborates with ESD advisors, layout designers, and the digital team that designs the chip’s digital logic.“I work with them to make sure my analog circuits and their digital blocks work together correctly,” she says. “No two days look exactly the same.”In 2024 she was recognized with the company’s Impact Award for her “exceptional work on a critical project with significant cross-functional business impact.”Presenting the final productAshwath was selected to represent Analog at events after a senior leader encouraged her to ask for high-visibility opportunities, she says.“Most of my time is spent on designing circuits and simulations,” she says. “At CES, I stood in front of customers, engineers, and members of the press, explaining our technology and answering questions on the spot.”The earbuds she demonstrated monitor minute vibrations from a user’s heart and lungs, according to the Analog website. The vibrations can detect arrhythmia, a leaky heart valve, or fluid in the lungs.“Hearables are evolving from playing back audio to becoming health-monitoring platforms,” she says. “The ear turns out to be a good location for picking up physiological signals, so these devices can capture vital signs while someone is simply wearing them normally.“The hard part is achieving high signal quality. The signals you’re trying to detect are very small and buried in the noise from the person’s movements and the surrounding environment.“That’s where analog front-end design becomes critical. Extracting a meaningful signal from a noisy real-world environment is fundamentally an analog problem.”Being face-to-face with customers at the conference was new to her.“What struck me most was seeing how people react to the technology,” she says. “When you’re designing a block, you’re focused on specifications and margins. At CES, after explaining what the product does, I had a better understanding of why it matters to them.“That connection between the circuit work and the final product is something you don’t always see from the design bench.”Since the CES, Ashwath has presented other technologies she’s worked on. At the annual National Association of Music Merchants show in Anaheim, Calif., she demonstrated the A2B Automotive Audio Bus to the audio industry. The bus uses a low-cost unshielded twisted-pair cable to carry multichannel digital audio, control data, synchronized clock signals, and power in fewer than 50 microseconds, according to Analog.“IEEE connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”At the company’s Global Technology Conference—an internal event held in Boston that draws engineers from the company’s more than 50 sites around the world—Ashwath led a demonstration of its solutions for augmented reality smart glasses.“Each of these events has a different audience,” she says. “Learning to explain my technical work to different people has become a skill I’ve acquired.”The most rewarding part of her job, she says, is seeing the end result of her work.“You spend months on a design, and there’s a long wait between finishing it and finding out whether your instincts were right,” she says. “When the measurements match what you simulated, that’s the most satisfying moment in this job.“The other part is knowing my work ends up in a real product. The circuits I design go into devices people actually use every day.”Giving back to the communityLike many engineers, Ashwath joined IEEE to access research published in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. It keeps her current in a field that keeps moving, she says.During her first year of membership, in 2021, she discovered other perks including networking and educational opportunities.“IEEE connects you to a community outside your own company,” she says. “Attending lectures and technical talks exposes you to approaches and problems you wouldn’t encounter in your own work.”She eventually began seeking out volunteer opportunities, specifically with IEEE conferences and journals, because they are “how you stay current with what’s happening in circuits and systems beyond your own day-to-day work,” she says.“As an analog designer,” she says, “being connected to that broader community matters. The field moves, and you need a way to keep learning from it.”She serves as a peer reviewer of papers for several IEEE conferences including the IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems and the IEEE International Midwest Symposium on Circuits and Systems. ISCAS is the flagship conference of the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society. MWSCAS is the oldest U.S. conference on the technologies.“Someone has to assess whether submitted work is technically sound and worth presenting,” she says, “and that only happens if practicing engineers are willing to put in the time.”The combination of learning from the community and contributing to it is what makes her membership worthwhile, she says.“Analog design is a field where you’re always learning. Just when you feel you understand one architecture, there’s another one to learn,” she says. “Being an active learner isn’t optional in this field; it’s the requirement, and being part of the IEEE community helps with that.“IEEE also connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry.“Reviewing papers means reading what researchers are working on, which is often quite different from how the same problems get approached in a product environment. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”
